How much can you discount a tutoring package before it costs you money?

The instinct is to keep a package discount at or below your no-show rate, so the guaranteed revenue covers what the discount gives up. That protects revenue. It does not protect your hourly pay if you owe a makeup on a missed session — that drops by about the discount percentage no matter what your no-show rate is, and the two worked examples below show why.

Open the free tutor package pricing calculator

The rule the calculator applies

With a makeup owed on a miss, every package session is eventually worked, however many were missed the first time. So package hours always equal the full session count, and package effective hourly pay always equals your discounted per-session rate — full stop. Pay-per-session hourly pay does not move with your no-show rate either, for the opposite reason: a missed slot is simply unpaid and unworked, so revenue and hours shrink together and the rate per hour stays at your full single-session price. The no-show rate decides which pricing model wins on raw revenue. It has no say at all in which one pays more per hour.

Worked example: a 25% discount against a 10% no-show rate

A tutor charges $60 per single session and sells a 10-session package for $450 — a 25% per-session discount. About 10% of booked sessions are no-shows, and a missed package session is always made up rather than forfeited. Sessions run 60 minutes with no extra prep or travel time.

Pay-per-sessionPackage
Revenue for this block$540.00$450.00
Hours actually worked9.0010.00
Effective hourly pay$60.00/hr$45.00/hr

Here the 25% discount is deeper than the 10% no-show rate, so the package loses on both lines: $90.00 less revenue and $15.00 less per hour than simply charging $60 per session and letting a no-show free that slot.

Worked example: the discount matched exactly to the no-show rate

Same tutor, same 10% no-show rate and makeup policy — but this time the package is priced at $540 for those 10 sessions, a 10% discount that exactly matches the no-show rate, which is the boundary most pricing advice treats as "safe."

Pay-per-sessionPackage
Revenue for this block$540.00$540.00
Hours actually worked9.0010.00
Effective hourly pay$60.00/hr$54.00/hr

Revenue is now identical — the discount no longer costs the tutor anything on that line. Hourly pay still is not: $54.00 an hour against $60.00 an hour, a $6.00 gap that matches the 10% discount almost exactly. Matching the discount to the no-show rate fixes the revenue problem. It does nothing for the hourly one, because with a makeup owed the package still pays its discounted rate on every one of the 10 hours, while pay-per-session's rate per hour never depended on the no-show rate to begin with.

What actually protects your hourly pay

Only two changes touch the hourly number at all. Charge no discount — price the package at exactly the single-session rate times the session count, and package hourly pay equals pay-per-session hourly pay exactly. Or stop owing a makeup on a missed package session: a forfeited miss frees the same hour under either pricing model, so package hours match pay-per-session hours exactly and the package only ever wins, on revenue, without ever touching your rate per hour. Anything short of one of those two changes leaves the discount sitting in your hourly pay, whatever it does to your no-show math.

Common questions

If my package discount is smaller than my no-show rate, am I safe?

Your package revenue is protected at that point — it will match or beat pay-per-session revenue. Your effective hourly pay is not protected. With a makeup owed on every miss, the package pays your discounted per-session rate on every hour, whatever your no-show rate is, so a 10% discount still costs you about 10% of your hourly pay even when your no-show rate is also 10%.

Why does the no-show rate not set a safe floor for hourly pay too?

Because with a makeup owed, every package session is eventually worked no matter how many were missed the first time — so package hours always equal the full session count, and package hourly pay always equals the discounted per-session rate. Pay-per-session hourly pay is unaffected by the no-show rate for the same reason in reverse: a missed slot is simply unpaid and unworked, so revenue and hours shrink together and the rate per hour stays at your full single-session price. The no-show rate changes which one wins on revenue. It does not change the hourly math at all.

What actually protects my hourly pay, then?

Two things, and only these two. Charge no discount at all, so the package's per-session rate equals your single-session price. Or stop owing a makeup on a miss, so a package no-show frees the same hour a pay-per-session no-show would — package hours then match pay-per-session hours exactly, and the package only ever wins, on revenue, without touching your hourly rate.

Does a bigger package justify a bigger discount?

Not on the hourly-pay math. Package size does not appear in the effective-hourly comparison at all — ten sessions or thirty at the same discount and the same makeup policy cost you the same percentage of hourly pay. A bigger package only changes how much total revenue is riding on that same percentage.

TUTOR PACKAGE PRICING CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Your package protects revenue. Does it protect your hourly pay?

A discounted prepaid session package guarantees you get paid even if a student no-shows. If a missed session also earns a free makeup rather than being forfeited, you still work that hour eventually — so the discount you gave to sell the package applies to every hour once they are all delivered, not just the ones attended the first time. This calculator compares your package to plain pay-per-session pricing on both revenue and effective hourly pay, so you know which one you are actually choosing.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Compare package vs. pay-per-session

Enter a single-session price, a package size and price, then click Compare.

Comparison

Pricing modelRevenueHours workedEffective pay

Copies both models' revenue, hours, and effective hourly pay, the deltas, and the disclaimer as plain text.

What this does and doesn't do

This applies the numbers you enter to one representative block of sessions — it does not track which specific student owes a makeup, does not schedule anything, and does not predict any one student's actual attendance. Treat the result as the arithmetic behind a pricing decision, not a record of any real student's account.

Common questions

Does a prepaid session package actually protect my income?

It protects your revenue: the student has already paid, so a no-show does not cost you that session's fee. It does not automatically protect your hourly pay. If your package promises a makeup for a missed session, you still work that hour eventually — the discount you gave to sell the package is paid on every hour once all of them are delivered, not just the hours actually attended the first time.

When does a package pay worse per hour than charging per session?

Whenever the package's per-session discount is deeper than your no-show rate and a missed session earns a free makeup. Under pay-per-session, a no-show simply frees that slot — you are not paid for it, but you also do not work it. Under a package with makeup owed, that slot is rescheduled rather than freed, so you work the same total hours as if nobody had missed a session, at the discounted rate.

So should I stop offering makeups?

This calculator does not tell you what policy to run — that depends on what keeps students booking with you. It tells you the arithmetic consequence of each policy so the tradeoff (guaranteed revenue vs. protected hourly pay) is a choice you make on purpose, not a side effect of a discount you picked to sound attractive.

What no-show rate should I use if I don't track one?

Use your best honest estimate from recent memory, or run the comparison at a couple of different rates (for example 5% and 20%) to see how sensitive the result is. The point is the relationship between your discount and your no-show rate, not a precise historical figure.

Is this scheduling software or tax advice?

No. It applies the numbers you enter to one representative block of sessions — it does not track which student owes a makeup, does not schedule anything, and is not tax, legal, or financial advice.

I already compare these in a spreadsheet — why use this instead?

A spreadsheet catches the revenue comparison fine. It usually misses the hours a makeup guarantee still owes on a missed session, which is where a discounted package can quietly pay worse per hour worked. See this calculator vs. a spreadsheet for a worked example.

I keep my discount at or below my no-show rate — isn't that safe?

It protects your revenue. It does not protect your hourly pay if you owe a makeup on a missed session — see how much you can discount a package before it costs you money for the worked example where a discount matched exactly to the no-show rate still costs $6.00 an hour.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

Most tutors who compare a prepaid package against pay-per-session pricing do it with one spreadsheet line: package price against sessions times single-session price. That line answers a revenue question. It does not answer whether the package pays better per hour actually worked — and when a package promises a makeup for a missed session, those two questions can point in opposite directions.

What each one is for

A spreadsheet is fine for the revenue comparison, and most tutors already have one: package price in one cell, sessions times single price in another. What it leaves out, unless someone builds it in on purpose, is hours — specifically, that a package with a makeup guarantee still owes every session eventually, so a no-show does not shrink the hours worked the way it does under pay-per-session.

This calculator takes your single-session price, package size and price, no-show rate, and whether a miss earns a makeup, and reports revenue and effective hourly pay for both models side by side, plus the package price that would clear a target hourly rate.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Which pricing model brings in more revenue?A spreadsheet answers this fine — it's one subtraction.
Which pricing model pays more per hour actually worked?Only if the sheet also converts a makeup policy into hours, which most don't. This calculator does it directly.
Can a deep package discount plus a makeup guarantee pay worse than full price?Yes — this page's worked example below shows exactly that case.
Does either one tell me what to charge?Neither. Both apply only the numbers you enter.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Worked example: a $60 session, a 10-for-$450 package, 10% no-shows, makeup owed

A tutor charges $60 per single session, and sells a package of 10 sessions for $450 — a 25% per-session discount. From recent memory, about 10% of booked sessions are no-shows, and the tutor's package policy is to reschedule (not forfeit) a missed session. Each session runs 60 minutes with 15 minutes of prep, so 75 minutes of work per session delivered.

Pay-per-sessionPackage
Revenue for this block$540.00$450.00
Hours actually worked11.2512.50
Effective hourly pay$48.00/hr$36.00/hr

A revenue-only spreadsheet line sees $450 versus $540 and stops at "the package brings in less, but it's guaranteed up front." It never surfaces the second, sharper fact: because the missed session is made up rather than forfeited, the tutor ends up working more hours for less money — $36.00 an hour against $48.00 an hour charging full price per session and letting a no-show simply free that slot. The 25% discount is deeper than the 10% no-show rate it was meant to cover, and a makeup guarantee turns that gap into an hourly-pay loss rather than a wash.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet compare package pricing against pay-per-session?

It can compare revenue in one line: package price against sessions times single-session price. What it usually does not do on its own is account for the hours a makeup guarantee still owes on a missed session, which is the part that decides whether the package actually pays better per hour worked.

Why does a revenue-only comparison miss the real answer?

Because a package guarantees revenue but, with a makeup owed, does not reduce hours the way a pay-per-session no-show does. A no-show under pay-per-session simply frees that slot, unpaid and unworked. A no-show under a package with makeup owed is rescheduled, not forfeited, so every hour is eventually worked at the discounted rate. A spreadsheet cell comparing two revenue totals never sees that difference.

What would I have to build into a spreadsheet to catch this?

A row for whether a missed session is made up or forfeited, a formula that converts that choice into hours actually worked (not just sessions attended), and effective hourly pay for both pricing models from those hours — then keep that formula correct every time the no-show rate, discount, or makeup policy changes. This calculator runs that model directly and shows revenue and effective hourly pay side by side.

Does either one tell me what to charge?

No. Both a spreadsheet and this calculator only compute the consequence of numbers you supply — your single-session price, package size and price, no-show rate, and makeup policy. Neither one knows your market or your students; you decide what to charge.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is uploaded.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.

Nothing here says or implies that a spreadsheet is a bad way to track your pricing — it is a different job: a formula you build and maintain yourself, where this calculator applies the hours-aware comparison for you and shows the breakdown.
